content:
I want to talk about how to define output of turing machines. The current code in CSLib does the following:

/--
The initial configuration corresponding to a list in the input alphabet.
Note that the entries of the tape constructed by `BiTape.mk₁` are all `some` values.
This is to ensure that distinct lists map to distinct initial configurations.
-/
def initCfg (tm : SingleTapeTM Symbol) (s : List Symbol) : tm.Cfg := ⟨some tm.q₀, BiTape.mk₁ s⟩

/-- The final configuration corresponding to a list in the output alphabet.
(We demand that the head halts at the leftmost position of the output.)
-/
def haltCfg (tm : SingleTapeTM Symbol) (s : List Symbol) : tm.Cfg := ⟨none, BiTape.mk₁ s⟩

/-- A proof of `tm` outputting `l'` on input `l`. -/
def Outputs (tm : SingleTapeTM Symbol) (l l' : List Symbol) : Prop :=
  ReflTransGen tm.TransitionRelation (initCfg tm l) (haltCfg tm l')

That is, there is a unique configuration of a turing machine that represents the state of "has halted and outputs the list l'". In my opinion, this has the downside that there are computations on turing machines that halt, but have no output in the sense that there is no l' such that Outputs tm l l' is provable.

In my experience so far I found it more desirable to have a function output {Symbol : Type} (tm : SingleTapeTM) : tm.Cfg → List Symbol which yields the output of an arbitrary configuration. Usually, this is then defined as the maximum sublist starting at the head and extending to the right without none values. This makes some definitions easier, but it makes compositions of functions more complicated because you need to do manual cleanup of the turing machine now.

In literature, both variants are present. Some sources require only the output to remain on the tape, others define what "the output" is meant to mean for any current tape configuration (with finite support). Obviously they yield the same notion of computability up to poly-time, so in that sense this definition does not change our theory, just how we need to deal with it during formalization.

I would be in favor of introducing such an output function also to CSLib and define output predicates based on that, but would be happy to receive further comments / opinions / arguments on which design decision to make here.

Further down the line, I would also find it interesting to define both versions and proof their equivalence (up to poly time).

I am in favour of this change. Composability as functions is not the first and most important result, so I think it’s fine if this is not as immediate. There are results that say that a tm can be turned into a tm that clears all its (work) tapes and moves the heads to the left end of the tape content (if any), and if i remember correctly, this only incurs at most linear cost in time and zero cost in space. Such a normalisation lemma can then be proved to obtain equivalence. Note that if we are talking about machines with a write-only output tape, then the output is to the left of the head, but I guess that should not be a problem.
